Mr. Saman's brow furrowed deeply. *Who is that young man?* he thought. A memory tried to struggle up from the dark trench of his mind, searching for a familiar name, but a thick fog quickly descended and swallowed it whole. Empty.
The old man blinked and looked up, waiting in peaceful ignorance, at the exact second the brass bell above his door prepared to ring.

sides.title: The Misdirected Address
body: The letter arrived on the wrong day, in the wrong city, traveling a long journey tracing the trail of mail-forwarding services from one obsolete address to another, until it arrived in the hands of the man who had long stopped waiting for it. The envelope was frayed, covered in the scribbles of wrong routes and stamps from various post offices—a naked testament to a cowardly habit Banyu never dared to admit. He always swore he didn't want to be found, yet in every city he left behind, he secretly always registered his new address. He never truly locked his door. And precisely because of that denial, when he saw the original handwriting beneath the piled-up postmarks, he had to sit down.

Banyu recognized the handwriting before he read his own name. Slanted, slow, sewn letter by letter like someone afraid of making a mistake. Twelve years he hadn't seen it, and he was seventeen again instantly, standing at the door of the tailor shop with a backpack on his back, saying *Father, I'm leaving now*, and waiting for something that never came.

He didn't open it. He placed it on the table, face down, as if words facing the floor had less power. Then he stared at it from across the room, from the same chair where he used to stare at the phone that didn't ring and the mailbox he checked every morning with a hope he despised within himself.

Twelve years, and this was the first thing his Father had sent. Not when he graduated. Not when he married. Not when he divorced and sat alone on the floor of his empty apartment, staring at the only chair Sari left behind, and almost—almost—wrote back home. Nothing for twelve years. Then, suddenly, a letter.

Banyu knew about that drawer, and that was what hurt him the most. As a child he had opened it, once, out of curiosity, and found it full—envelopes piled up, some for customers, some for distant relatives, and one small pile with a single word on each face: *Mother*. His Father wrote to his vanished wife and kept every single letter, because sending meant acknowledging the possibility of not getting a reply, and his Father could better bear his own silence than the silence that came from the other side as an answer.
Banyu swore, at age seventeen, he would not be that man. He would be the man who sent. Who spoke. Who left.
So he left. And for twelve years he proved, city by city, that he had succeeded in becoming the opposite of his father.
The letter on the table, face down, which he hadn't yet opened, was the first thing that made him doubt he had proven anything at all.
He didn't open it that night. He put on his coat and went out walking, because walking was the only inheritance from his mother that he didn't regret.

People think wanderers walk to see the world. Banyu walked so as not to be in one place long enough for that place to have the chance to demand something from him. As he walked down the wet sidewalks, the cities he had stopped in over the last twelve years came back to haunt him—not in order, because memories have no order, but as smells and sounds and a few people who, only tonight, he suspected had tried to tell him the same thing, and failed, because that same thing simply cannot be told. It can only be found, too late, alone.
There was the port city where he ran out of money in his first month of wandering, and was forced to work in a watch shop owned by an old woman who was deaf in one ear.

But it wasn't the watches that Banyu remembered tonight. Not the stopped watches lined up on the dark shelves, not the woman's words about guarding minutes. What he remembered was this: that for the six months in that shop, the old half-deaf woman called him to dinner every Sunday, and Banyu, who was just seventeen and hard and arrogant in his loneliness, always refused. He didn't want to be helped. He didn't want to be made to feel at home. Feeling at home is an anchor, and he came to throw anchors, not drop them.

Until one morning, Banyu decided to run. Secretly, before dawn, without saying goodbye. As he prepared to leave, he found a banana leaf parcel filled with warm rice and side dishes on his work desk. The old deaf woman had apparently woken up much earlier just to cook provisions for him. But Banyu couldn't even be bothered to take the parcel. He just left it there on the table, sneaked out, and left the old woman to wake up to his absence.

Tonight, twelve years later, Banyu's chest suddenly tightened. He stopped walking. His breath raced as a realization hit him: in that port city, he had left that old woman in the exact same way his mother had left him. Before dawn. Without a sound. Leaving something on the table in exchange for a goodbye he couldn't bear.
His mother had also left something on the table, that morning, long ago. Banyu was nine. He never knew what it was, because his Father found it first, and hid it, and never showed it to him.
There was the village in the mountains where the air was too thin for much talking, where he worked for a mapmaker named Mr. Galih who drew maps of people instead of maps of places.

Banyu still kept the map Mr. Galih made for him—not because he cherished it, but because he had never managed to truly throw it away. Twice he thought he had thrown it out; twice he found it again at the bottom of his bag. Eventually, he stopped trying.

What Mr. Galih had said back then—that Banyu's line was straight, moving away, never curving back, that he wasn't heading toward anything but was just running away and calling it an adventure—Banyu angrily rejected it at the time. But it wasn't those sentences that haunted him tonight. What haunted him was the small thing Mr. Galih did at the end, which he only understood now.

After drawing Banyu's map, Mr. Galih drew one more map, on a separate piece of paper, and didn't show it. Banyu caught only a brief glimpse of it, before the old man put it away: a map with lines that curved, not straight—starting from one point, reaching far, then returning to the same point, over and over. Banyu assumed it was another customer's map. He didn't ask. Young people don't ask about the sadness of old people; they are too busy thinking sadness belongs solely to themselves.

Only tonight did Banyu suspect—only suspected, he would never know for sure—that the curved map was Mr. Galih's own map. Or the map of someone who had once traveled all that distance for Mr. Galih, secretly, without Mr. Galih knowing. And that the old man kept those two maps side by side—the straight and the curved—not to show off, but because he had learned the very thing Banyu was fiercely rejecting: that for every person walking straight away, there is a possibility, somewhere behind them, someone curving home every night, and those two lines share the exact same points, and neither of them knows the other line exists.

Mr. Galih didn't explain this. He only kept those two maps, and let Banyu leave with one straight map in his bag, and never told him about the curved one. Perhaps because he knew—as old people often know—that there are things which, if you tell them to young people, go in one ear and out the other, and only reside in their chests years later, when the person themselves is old enough to discover them.
And there was the big city where he married Sari, and where he found, with a horror that grew slowly like a rising tide, that he had failed.

Sari was full of words, and at first Banyu loved her exactly for that—around someone that fluent, he was free from the obligation to speak. But Banyu never truly told Sari anything deep. About his mother, he said "already passed away"—a lie that was easier than "left". About his father, he said nothing. About why he couldn't sleep if the windows were shut tight, about why he always sat facing the door, about why every time Sari packed a suitcase for a work trip, something in his chest hardened into a stone until Sari came home—he didn't tell her a single thing. He loved Sari as fully as he could, but he loved her from a locked room, and he slid food and warmth and loyalty through the gap under the door, and called that a marriage.

Sari lasted seven years. That was longer than was deserved. On the last night, she didn't yell. She only said, while folding clothes into a suitcase with very calm hands: "I know you love me. That's what hurts the most. I could live with someone who doesn't love me. I cannot live with someone who loves me but decides I am not allowed inside. You love me the way a person loves something through a window, Banyu. And I am tired of being the scenery."
Then she lifted her suitcase, and stood at the door, and said—with a voice that finally broke—"I'm leaving now."
And Banyu, who his entire life swore he would not be his father, who wandered thousands of kilometers to prove he was not a man who let people leave in silence—
Banyu nodded.

He just nodded. Exactly like his father at the shop door, twelve years earlier. A thousand sentences crowded his chest—*don't, stay, I will learn, give me time, I don't know how but I will learn*—and not a single one came out. The door closed. Sari left. And Banyu stood in the apartment that suddenly only contained one chair, and understood that he had walked halfway around the world only to turn around and find his father already waiting for him inside, patient, all along—not in his hometown, but in his own chest, like a black king lost from the board but still dictating the entire game.

That was the last city before this one. Banyu never told anyone about it. He packed, and moved, and called it a new job. A straight line. Moving away. Always. Leaving only one secret visit to the post office to renew his forwarding address once again—an irony of someone walking away, yet secretly always leaving breadcrumbs to be followed.

Banyu returned to his rented apartment near dawn. The letter with the frayed envelope adorned with dozens of forwarding stamps was still lying on the table. Banyu sat down, turned the envelope over, and opened it. His hands trembled slightly, and he looked at his own hands with a gentle horror—the tremor was exactly the same as the tremor of his father's hands holding fabric scissors.
On the lined paper, four sentences were written. Sewn letter by letter, very neatly: *Son, I am well here. The shop is still open. I am still sewing. If you have time, come home.*
However, at the bottom of the paper, written in slightly faded ink, driven by a great courage that came too late in life, there was one additional sentence:
*And if you cannot come home, it's alright. I just want you to know I am proud. Go as far as you want. I am perfectly fine.*

Banyu bowed his head, covered his face with both hands, and burst into tears. His body shook violently in the middle of the apartment's silence. He wasn't crying because his father asked him to come home. He broke down precisely because, for the first time in the history of their petrified family, his father let him go. Because that was what Banyu had been waiting for for twelve years without realizing it. Not a call to return, but the blessing to leave.
That morning, before the sun fully rose, Banyu took a piece of paper and a pen.

*Dad. I've been angry at you for twelve years, and only this dawn I realized I was angry at the wrong address. I thought I was angry because you never stopped me from leaving. When in fact I was angry because I was waiting for you to say I was allowed to leave, and you never said it, until today.*
*I also want to ask for one thing. The note Mother left that morning. I know you hid it. I understand now that you hid it because it hurt you. But I am old enough now, Dad. I want to read it.*
*I am coming home this week, Dad. Not because you told me to. But precisely because you set me free.*
Banyu folded the paper, put it into an envelope, and that very morning, he sent it.

The journey home took four days. The train happened to stop quite a while in the port city that had once been his first refuge. Banyu got off from the station, walked down the smoky streets, and found the watch shop where he had once worked. The shop was still there, but its owner was now a middle-aged man he didn't recognize.
"Where is the old woman who used to own this place?" asked Banyu.

"Already passed away, Sir. A few years ago," replied the new owner. "But she bequeathed an odd rule—all watches that are completely dead cannot be fixed, cannot be sold, they must be left on the back shelf."

Banyu's chest buzzed strangely. The half-deaf woman—whose banana leaf cooking he had abandoned over a decade ago—had died in solitude. Banyu went in, stood among hundreds of dead watches on the back shelf. He bought one, an old pocket watch whose hands were frozen on God knows whose minute, and brought it with him, deciding that even a foreign minute deserved to be guarded.

He didn't know—and would never know—that on the very back shelf of that shop, among the watches, was an empty glass bottle that wasn't allowed to be thrown away, which guarded the old woman's own minutes. Banyu walked right past it and didn't see it. It is almost always like that: we pass in front of the most important minutes of other people without ever knowing those minutes are there. Every stranger passing us by is carrying an invisible stopped watch, and we never know what time it says.
On the fourth day, Banyu arrived at the narrow alley that was barely passed by people, and stood in front of the tailor shop whose sign was increasingly faded.
He stood for a long time. Then, through the frosted window, he saw an old man in front of a chessboard, moving a piece with a trembling hand, playing against himself on a quiet afternoon.
Banyu took a breath. A thousand sentences crowded his chest. But this time he would not nod and be silent. He opened the door. The bell rang. The old man looked up.
And Banyu understood, in that fraction of a second, before a single word was spoken, that he was at the wrong address again.

Because there was a pause. A pause that was too long. The old man's eyes searched his face—searching, tracing, with wrinkles that slowly deepened—and found nothing. There was no flash of recognition. There was no name rising to the trembling lips. Only a very old man looking at a strange man who entered his shop right before closing time, with the empty politeness of someone greeting a customer.
"Come in, Sir," his father said. "What would you like sewn?"

Banyu stood at the threshold, with the letter in his pocket and a stopped watch in his hand and twelve years on his back, and couldn't say anything. Not because of the silence he inherited. But because there was no longer a drawer on the other side to be opened. There was no longer someone holding onto sentences for him. The disease that took the old man's memory—who knows when it started, who knows how long, the letter was probably written on one of the last days when he still remembered he had a son—had emptied the drawer before Banyu arrived to read it.
He had walked all around the round earth, and arrived exactly one minute after the watch stopped.

Banyu didn't correct him. He didn't say *Dad, it's me*. He was old enough to know that forcing someone to remember you is cruelty, not love—that demanding recognition from an already empty drawer will only make the old man afraid, ashamed, lost in his own shop.
So he did the only thing that could still be done by someone who arrived too late. He came inside. He sat down. And he said, with a voice he kept light even though his chest was collapsing:
"I want to learn to sew, Sir. If you wouldn't mind teaching me. I can pay."

And the old man's face—the face that didn't recognize his son—lit up with something older than memory, something that lived in the hands and not in the head. "I can, I can," he said, and there was a warmth there, a warmth that didn't know to whom it was directed and gave it anyway. "Sit here. I'll teach you. I used to have a son, wanted to teach him this..."—he stopped, his brow furrowing at something that slipped in and vanished—"...but he grew up too fast. Children always grow up too fast."
"Yes, Sir," Banyu said, and his voice barely broke. "Always."
So Banyu stayed.

He didn't send another reply letter; there was no use. He rented a room in the same alley and came to the shop every day, and the old man taught him to sew—taught him over and over, because every few days he forgot he had ever taught him, and started from the beginning, and Banyu learned the same things repeatedly with a patience he never knew he had, because every repetition was one more afternoon with his father, and he wouldn't waste a single one.

Sometimes the old man called him by the wrong name. Sometimes, very rarely, on certain afternoons when the light fell a certain way, he would look at Banyu for too long and say, "You remind me of someone," and Banyu would just smile and say, "Oh yeah, Sir?" and never finished the sentence for him, because some recognition, if forced, will shatter, and is better left hanging, warm and unfinished, like a watch that stops at a good minute.

They played chess in the afternoons. The old man was always black, always with the button king. And one day Banyu took out the stopped pocket watch he bought in the port city, and placed it on the side of the board, and didn't explain why. The old man looked at it, then nodded as if understanding something Banyu himself hadn't fully grasped, and said, "Good. Everyone should have one. A watch that has stopped." Then he moved his piece, and lost as usual, and smiled.

Banyu never found his mother's note. He looked for it, slowly, among the drawers and boxes and tins of buttons, on the days when his father took an afternoon nap. He didn't find it. Maybe the old man had destroyed it years ago. Maybe he hid it so well that the memory of where he hid it left along with his other memories. Maybe the note was still there, somewhere in that shop, waiting, and one day would fall from behind something when Banyu was no longer looking for it.

Banyu decided to stop searching. He was old enough to know that some addresses are permanently swapped, some letters simply never arrive, some drawers are indeed empty when we finally dare to open them—and that life, strangely, doesn't become unbearable because of it. He would never know why his mother left. His father would never know his son came home. Sari would never know that at that apartment door, behind the nod, there were a thousand sentences.

But Banyu knew now. That was what changed. He had walked around the entire round earth and arrived one minute late, and found that arriving one minute late is not the same as never arriving. He arrived. The old man didn't know who was sewing beside him every afternoon, but he was no longer sewing alone. And perhaps that was the entirety of the blessing that could ever be given by two people who both could never speak: not words, in the end, but presence—one afternoon, then another afternoon, in a cramped shop, among fabric and thread and a chessboard with a button king, two men guarding each other from the exact same silence, one who forgot and one who finally, belatedly, chose to stay.
Outside, the afternoon slowly descended upon the narrow alley. Inside, the old man moved his piece, and lost, and chuckled, and said to the stranger he cared for without knowing why:
"Come again tomorrow, okay, son. I'm happy to have a friend."
And Banyu, who his entire life left, said the thing he his entire life never said to anyone, and this time he said it, and this time he would keep it:
"Yes, Sir. Tomorrow I'll come again."

sides.title: The Woman Who Counted Backwards
body: The first thing Maryam counted was the spoons. It was the fourth morning of her marriage. She opened the kitchen drawer in their new house and counted the teaspoons—twelve, in pairs, a gift from someone or other—and felt, for a reason she couldn't explain, relieved. Twelve was a full number. Even. Enough for guests who hadn't arrived, children who hadn't been born, years that hadn't been lived. She closed the drawer and didn't think about it again for years.

She didn't know, that morning, that she would spend the rest of her marriage counting. That counting would become her way of surviving, then her way of tormenting herself, then the only language left to measure something that had no units. She just closed the drawer, and brewed tea for two, and waited for her husband to come down.

Saman proposed to her without words. He sewed Maryam a dress—secretly, with measurements he somehow knew exactly—and handed it over with eyes that didn't dare lift from the floor. Maryam understood that the dress was a proposal, because the man had no sentences to propose with, and she accepted.

At twenty-two, she thought a man's silence was depth. She thought behind a person who didn't talk much there must be something massive, stored away, waiting for the one right person to open it up. She thought she would be that person.

She wasn't completely wrong. There was something massive behind Saman's silence. Maryam spent ten years trying to reach it, and found that the massive thing was real—she saw it, sometimes, in her husband's eyes, something full and urgent and clearly wanting to get out. But there was no way there. Not a locked door. Something worse: a wall built so neatly that even the one inside forgot there used to be a door.

She couldn't hate Saman, and that was what was most exhausting. If Saman were abusive, she would have a reason, and a reason is a grip. But Saman was gentle. He saved the best cut on the plate for Maryam. He sewed Maryam the most beautiful clothes in town, which Maryam wore to parties where other women praised her and told her how lucky she was, how attentive her husband was, and Maryam smiled and agreed and went home to a silent house and felt like a liar.

Because no one believes in the loneliness of a woman who has everything. It is a loneliness you have to deny every day, until the denial itself becomes a full-time job, until you forget which is you and which is your denial.
She counted sentences. It was a habit that grew without her deciding to.

Not sentences like "where's the salt" or "close the shop, it's going to rain". The other sentences—sentences that mentioned feelings, that mentioned Maryam as Maryam and not as part of the household machinery. Some days she got one. Most days, zero.

She hoarded those numbers the way people hoard debts. And she hated herself for counting—because counting means measuring, and measuring someone's love is a small betrayal against them, and Saman didn't deserve to be betrayed even secretly, even just inside her head. But she couldn't stop. Numbers were the only way she could prove to herself that what she felt was real, that she wasn't crazy, that the emptiness she felt wasn't her fabrication—because if she could count it, she existed.

And this was what she didn't admit until years later: that Saman, perhaps, was also counting. That on the other side of the same wall, there was a man who was also measuring something he feared was insufficient, who was also hoarding numbers, who also felt like a liar at parties. That two people could live in one house, love sincerely, and each be convinced they were the only one who was lonely. Maryam never asked him about it. It was among the things she never asked, and that non-asking, she understood now, was the first brick of her own wall.
Then Banyu was born, and for a few years Maryam thought she was saved.

A baby is a creature full of sounds, full of demands, full of mouths that must be fed and eyes that light up when you enter a room. Maryam poured into her son all the words that had no place to go for ten years. She talked to Banyu all day long, even when the child was too small to understand, because finally there was someone listening.
But a child is not a vessel you can fill limitlessly without consequences. And one day, when Banyu was seven or eight, Maryam heard herself do something that made her hand stop mid-stir.

Banyu fell, scraped his knee, and cried. And Maryam, instead of asking "does it hurt?", found herself saying: "There, stop crying. It's okay. Hush." With a gentle voice. With a voice that was exactly—exactly—the voice used to muffle, to shut down, to teach a child that feelings are something better left unseen.
Her husband's voice. Coming out of her own mouth.

She stood in the kitchen with a spoon in her hand and realized she had been wrong all along. She thought Saman was silencing her. But silence, it turned out, didn't come from one direction and stay there; it spread, it was contagious, it entered the people living nearby and came out through their mouths without permission. Ten years beside a wall had made Maryam into a bit of a wall herself. And now that wall was building itself, brick by brick, around her eight-year-old son, through her own hands, through her own voice, through her own love.
That was the thing that finally made her decide to leave. Not her loneliness—she had already learned to bear her loneliness. But the horror of seeing herself pass it down.
I want to pause here for a moment, because this is the part you must know, and there is no clean way to say it.
Maryam left a nine-year-old child.

There is no paragraph that can make that painless. There is no excuse noble enough to make a child who wakes up and finds his mother gone feel less abandoned. Whatever Maryam thought she was saving by leaving, there is a boy who will grow up with a mother-shaped hole in his chest, who will check the mailbox for twelve years, who will hate something he doesn't understand until his hatred hardens into bone. Maryam knew this. She knew this the morning she left, and she knew this every morning after, and there wasn't a single day in the long rest of her life when she successfully completely convinced herself that she had been right.

That was what made her different from her husband, in the end. Not that she spoke and Saman was silent. But that Maryam carried her doubts with her, for a lifetime, open, incurable—while Saman buried his in a drawer. They both did damage. It was just that one refused to pretend the damage wasn't there.

Should she have stayed? I don't know. Maryam didn't know. Maybe staying would have made her a ghost, and made Banyu a child raised by a ghost, and made Banyu's future wife marry a ghost—a polite lineage of loneliness, straight down, unbroken. Or maybe that was just a story she fabricated to bear what she had already done. Maybe both are true. Maybe a decision can save someone and destroy someone else with the exact same action, and we are given no way to separate the two, and we still have to choose.
Maryam chose. And she paid for her choice every day until she died. That is not a justification. That is just what happened.
On the morning she left, she stood for a long time in her sleeping son's room.

She tried to wake him up. She swore she tried. There were entire paragraphs in her chest—paragraphs about the kitchen, about the wall, about why, about sorry—and she opened her mouth to speak them, and found, at the moment she needed it most, that her mouth closed.

Exactly like her husband's mouth at the shop door, years later, when that same boy would leave with a backpack on his back. Exactly like that boy's mouth, years further on, at the apartment door, when a woman named Sari would lift a suitcase. The same family. The same disease. And Maryam, who left precisely to break that chain, found herself at the final moment becoming just one more link in it—mute beside the person she most wanted to talk to.

So she wrote. Hands, sometimes, can do what mouths cannot. But even on paper her courage was only enough for a few lines—a tenth of what was in her chest, because a dam doesn't collapse just because you hand it a pen. She wrote a short note. She placed it on the kitchen table, under a cup, next to the drawer where twelve spoons now lived as eleven—because she took one, that morning, one teaspoon, without knowing why, perhaps just so there would be something from this house coming with her, something small and even and once full.
Then she kissed her son's forehead, very softly so as not to wake him—because if Banyu opened his eyes and looked at her, she knew she wouldn't have the strength to step outside—and she left.

That note never reached Banyu. Saman found it first, read it, and hid it. Not to protect his son. To protect himself—because among those short lines, Maryam had written a sentence about loving someone from a place she couldn't reach, and that sentence was a mirror Saman couldn't bear to face. So he buried it in the same drawer where he would later bury his own unsent letters. And his son grew up hating a silence, never knowing that the silence had once, a single time, tried to speak.

The world never asks what happens to the women who leave. Once the door closes, she ceases to exist; she becomes a hole in someone else's house, an absence shaped like a mother, an empty chair that other people stare at while wondering. But she didn't stop existing.
Maryam fled to a distant port city. A city that smelled of salt, fish guts, and ship oil.

The first few years were a brutal physical torment. She worked washing dishes at a stall by the pier. The wet and cold sea wind gnawed at her body. One night, she was struck by a severe fever for days. An infection attacked her left ear because it went untreated. When her fever broke, half of Maryam's world had become soundproof. She was officially half deaf.
Her hair turned white prematurely. Her back began to hunch from exhaustion. In her late thirties, her face wrinkled like a woman in her fifties.
She later worked for an old, nearly blind watch repairman, learning to disassemble and assemble gears and springs. When the owner died, Maryam inherited that small, dark shop.

Maryam liked watches. In that shop, hundreds of watches ticked simultaneously. That noisy *tick-tock* drowned out the silence that used to choke her in Saman's house. In the corner of her workbench, Maryam placed an empty glass bottle plugged with a cork. Every time she felt her chest tighten from missing Banyu, she didn't cry; she picked up a broken gear, and dropped it into the glass bottle. Saving a minute of her suffering, locking it up tightly.
Eight years after her flight, on a windy afternoon, her watch shop's door chime rang.

A teenage boy entered. He was perhaps barely seventeen. His clothes were shabby, and he carried a backpack soiled with street dust. He stood stiffly in front of the display case, his jaw clenched, his eyes staring down at the tiled floor.
"Can I help you, Son?" Maryam asked, tilting her head so her functioning right ear could hear.
"I need a job," the boy answered. His voice was low, hoarse, and restrained, as if he weren't used to using his vocal cords. "I can sweep, tidy the shelves. Anything."

Maryam looked at him for a long time. This port city was always full of wandering children running away from something. Every time she saw them, Maryam's chest throbbed with pain, because she always imagined Banyu. *This boy is the same age as Banyu now,* Maryam thought inwardly. She nodded, pointed to the broom in the corner of the room, and gave him a sleeping spot on a mat in the back storage room.
The boy was quiet. Very quiet.

He swept the floor almost without a sound. He ate his lunch rations in the corner of the room, always refusing to meet Maryam's eyes. Sometimes, when Maryam was hunched over installing a desk clock's gears, she glanced at the boy from behind her glasses. There was something in the boy that made Maryam's breath catch often. The way the boy stood with tense shoulders, the way he folded the dust cloth... somehow, those stiff movements evoked Maryam's memories of the way her husband held his fabric measuring tape in the past.

*This wandering boy must be running from a very cold house,* Maryam thought sympathetically, seeing how the boy locked himself away from the outside world. That thought made her haunted by a tremendous fear. *Is Banyu out there also drifting aimlessly like this boy? Is Banyu also freezing and building the same walls?*

Driven by her endless guilt towards her own biological son, Maryam tried to pour her attention into the quiet boy. Every Sunday, when the shop was closed, Maryam purposely cooked extra rice and side dishes.
"Eat with me, Son," Maryam called warmly from the wooden table in the back room, patting the empty chair next to her.

But the boy always froze in place. His face tensed as if kindness were something that threatened him. He shook his head stiffly, looked away, then stepped out of the shop and walked off to who-knows-where until late at night.

Every time the boy refused her dinner, Maryam swallowed her own food with an aching throat. The rejection slapped her. *Is this what it feels like to be ignored?* Maryam thought bitterly. *Is this what it feels like to stare at the back of someone who decides not to let you in?*
Six months the boy worked for her.
Then, one morning in the rainy season, Maryam awoke to a peculiar instinct. She walked slowly to the back storage room. The door was slightly ajar. The mat was empty. The shabby backpack was gone.
Maryam stood paralyzed at the threshold of the storage room. The dawn air blew in, bringing a cold chill. The boy had left. Secretly. Without saying goodbye.

Maryam walked unsteadily to the front desk. On the workbench where the boy usually organized the watches, she saw a banana leaf parcel. It was the rice and side dishes Maryam had woken up even earlier to cook, purposely placed there because she knew, from the look in the boy's eyes last night, that the boy was preparing to run away.

Maryam touched the banana leaf parcel that was slowly beginning to turn cold. The boy didn't take it. The boy rejected her offering until the very end. Refusing to have any ties whatsoever in this city.
Suddenly, Maryam's legs gave out. She slumped to the dusty wooden floor. Hugging her knees, Maryam cried without a sound until her entire chest convulsed.

The world truly knew how to punish her. Twelve years ago, she left the house before dawn, refusing to wake anyone, only leaving something on the table. Now, the universe forced her to feel the exact same pain, placing her precisely in the position of the one left behind.

In the midst of her agonizing sobs, Maryam's tears fell for Banyu. *Banyu... are you out there growing up into a boy this hard? Did you also leave the people who tried to care for you, exactly like this wandering boy left me?*

Maryam crawled to her workbench. With hands shaking violently, she opened the drawer, took out the cork-stoppered glass bottle, and dropped a broken metal gear into it. One minute full of regret, locked tightly at the bottom of the bottle.
Years passed since the nameless boy left. Maryam grew increasingly frail. Her hands were no longer strong enough to hold watch tweezers.

On a quiet morning, when she was in her extreme twilight years, Maryam sat near the open window of her shop. She took a piece of paper. She didn't know where Banyu was now, but she had to free this one thing from her chest.
She wrote slowly:

*Son. I will not explain why I left, because an explanation is just my way of asking you to understand, and you don't owe me any understanding. I just want you to know one small thing. I still remember your hand. Your little hand gripping the edge of the blanket when you slept. I left taking one teaspoon from our kitchen, and I still have it now. Every morning, when I stir my tea, I remember your hand.*

Maryam stopped writing for a moment. Her eyes gazed far off, staring at the empty workbench in the corner of the room, the place where that mute wandering boy once rejected all her attention. The sting of that dawn parting returned to disturb her.
Maryam swallowed hard, then added one final sentence into her letter:

*Out there, if there is someone who tries to offer you dinner or gives you shelter, please accept it, Son. Don't push them away. Don't let your heart turn to stone like the walls in our house used to be.*

She folded the letter. She wrote the address she had tracked down over the years through distant relatives and luck. She limped to the post office, sent it to her old, obsolete address, surrendering everything to fate. Calling out and being answered are two different things. Her only task was to call.

That afternoon, Maryam went home to her shop. She brewed hot tea in a glass cup. She took the 12th teaspoon—the spoon that once accompanied her in running away—and stirred her drink slowly. *Ting-ting-ting.* The sound of metal clinking against glass.

She sat smiling, watching hundreds of watches ticking. On the backmost shelf, the glass bottle filled with broken metal gears stood dusty. That morning, for the first time since the fourth morning of her marriage, she was no longer counting her mistakes. She took a deep breath, inhaling the morning air that smelled of sea salt, and for the first time, she felt even.

Maryam passed away peacefully in that chair during the following rainy season. She left carrying her peaceful ignorance. The shop was bequeathed with odd rules, but the dusty glass bottle on the back shelf remained untouched, guarding the frozen minutes, waiting patiently until over a decade later—when the shop's bell rang again, and a wandering man stepped in from the street, only to buy a dead pocket watch, and walked right past the single most precious minute of his own mother without ever knowing it.
